newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Soaring pound does not rule out UK rate rise.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Soaring pound does not rule out UK rate rise.

text.p: The British economy, buoyed by a wave of consumer spending, may force a pre-election interest rate rise even though the soaring pound is exerting a monetary tightening effect of its own, economists said on Tuesday.
Sterling has zoomed to 21-month highs against the German mark and an 11-month peak against the dollar.
That appreciation will dampen economic activity as exporters struggle with higher prices. And for the anti-inflation hawks, there is a double bonus as the pound's rise cuts import prices.
Nonetheless, with domestic high street spending continuing apace, some economists think an official interest rate rise is on the cards before elections which are due by May 1997.
"The Bank of England is quite happy to see this tightening by the back door but would still prefer an explicit rate rise," said Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"That would send a much more direct message to consumers and have much more impact," he said.

Minutes from the last two monthly monetary meetings between Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England Governor Eddie George have shown George would prefer base rates to be raised now, to 6.00 percent from 5.75.

The British Retail Consortium's latest survey, released early on Tuesday, showed retail sales up 5.2 percent year-on-year in September. That represents a slowdown from August's bumper month, but still healthy growth.

Barr forecast a 50 basis point increase in base rates early next year, despite intense pressure on finance minister Clarke from the ruling Conservative Party to keep rates low and cut taxes before elections.
He said Clarke may look to fight an election campaign on the basis of economic prudence, as a safe pair of hands, rather than trying to woo disaffected voters with rate and tax giveaways.
Others said the pound's rise was another, very useful string to Clarke's bow in his fight to keep rates on hold.

The old rule of thumb in the City is that a four percent appreciation in the pound is equivalent to a one percentage point increase in base rates. On a trade-weighted basis, sterling has leapt about five percent since early August.
Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets, said the last monetary meeting at which George is known to have suggested a rate rise was held on September 4.

"Since that meeting, sterling has appreciated by 3.3 percent. If you follow the old adage, we've had a 3/4 percentage point tightening since then and even if that equation is shaky, there's been a definite tightening."

Loynes said Clarke would use the pound's strength to back his case, not just because it will keep a lid on import prices but also because it could choke off Britain's nascent manufacturing recovery before it really gets started.
Two weeks ago, the Confederation of British Industry said it was too early to say if British exporters were feeling the pinch from the pound's climb.
"But if the pound's strength is sustained, then it could become more of a problem," Sudhir Junankar, the CBI's associate director of economic analysis, said.
Loynes said struggling manufacturers, not to mention political expediency, could even prompt one more rate cut.
"We still haven't ruled out a last rate cut out altogether. But we'd need to see a tight budget, continued strength in sterling and some good inflation numbers to get one," he said.
Barr said the pound was unlikely to keep sailing skywards, due to political uncertainties.
"If it shot through 2.50 marks it would relieve the pressure on Clarke but we don't expect that."
The pound touched 2.43 marks on Tuesday, up from around 2.27 in early August.
Barr said the Bank of England was primarily concerned with buoyant retail spending and the temptation for retailers to try and push through price increases.

But Loynes said the British consumer was still loathe to accept higher prices. "George has focused his argument on the consumer sector but it's still not clear consumers will be prepared to pay higher prices."
